#include <asm.h>
#include <csr.h>

.macro SAVE_CONTEXT
  addi sp, sp, -(OFFSET_SIZE)
  /* 
   * save all general purpose registers
   * register $zero, $sp, $tp are not stored here! 
   */
  sd ra, OFFSET_REG_RA(sp)
  sd gp, OFFSET_REG_GP(sp)
  sd t0, OFFSET_REG_T0(sp)
  sd t1, OFFSET_REG_T1(sp)
  sd t2, OFFSET_REG_T2(sp)
  sd s0, OFFSET_REG_S0(sp)
  sd s1, OFFSET_REG_S1(sp)
  sd a0, OFFSET_REG_A0(sp)
  sd a1, OFFSET_REG_A1(sp)
  sd a2, OFFSET_REG_A2(sp)
  sd a3, OFFSET_REG_A3(sp)
  sd a4, OFFSET_REG_A4(sp)
  sd a5, OFFSET_REG_A5(sp)
  sd a6, OFFSET_REG_A6(sp)
  sd a7, OFFSET_REG_A7(sp)
  sd s2, OFFSET_REG_S2(sp)
  sd s3, OFFSET_REG_S3(sp)
  sd s4, OFFSET_REG_S4(sp)
  sd s5, OFFSET_REG_S5(sp)
  sd s6, OFFSET_REG_S6(sp)
  sd s7, OFFSET_REG_S7(sp)
  sd s8, OFFSET_REG_S8(sp)
  sd s9, OFFSET_REG_S9(sp)
  sd s10, OFFSET_REG_S10(sp)
  sd s11, OFFSET_REG_S11(sp)
  sd t3, OFFSET_REG_T3(sp)
  sd t4, OFFSET_REG_T4(sp)
  sd t5, OFFSET_REG_T5(sp)
  sd t6, OFFSET_REG_T6(sp)

  /* save sstatus, sepc, stval, scause, sscratch on kernel stack */
  csrr t0, CSR_SSTATUS
  sd t0, OFFSET_REG_SSTATUS(sp)
  csrr t0, CSR_SEPC
  sd t0, OFFSET_REG_SEPC(sp)
  csrr t0, CSR_STVAL
  sd t0, OFFSET_REG_STVAL(sp)
  csrr t0, CSR_SCAUSE
  sd t0, OFFSET_REG_SCAUSE(sp)
  csrr t0, CSR_SSCRATCH
  sd t0, OFFSET_REG_SSCRATCH(sp)

  sd sp, PCB_KERNEL_SP(tp)
.endm

.macro RESTORE_CONTEXT
  ld sp, PCB_KERNEL_SP(tp)
  /* 
   * restore all registers and sstatus, sepc, stval, scause, sscratch
   * register $zero, $sp, $tp are not restored here!
   */
  ld ra, OFFSET_REG_RA(sp)
  ld gp, OFFSET_REG_GP(sp)
  ld t0, OFFSET_REG_T0(sp)
  ld t1, OFFSET_REG_T1(sp)
  ld t2, OFFSET_REG_T2(sp)
  ld s0, OFFSET_REG_S0(sp)
  ld s1, OFFSET_REG_S1(sp)
  ld a0, OFFSET_REG_A0(sp)
  ld a1, OFFSET_REG_A1(sp)
  ld a2, OFFSET_REG_A2(sp)
  ld a3, OFFSET_REG_A3(sp)
  ld a4, OFFSET_REG_A4(sp)
  ld a5, OFFSET_REG_A5(sp)
  ld a6, OFFSET_REG_A6(sp)
  ld a7, OFFSET_REG_A7(sp)
  ld s2, OFFSET_REG_S2(sp)
  ld s3, OFFSET_REG_S3(sp)
  ld s4, OFFSET_REG_S4(sp)
  ld s5, OFFSET_REG_S5(sp)
  ld s6, OFFSET_REG_S6(sp)
  ld s7, OFFSET_REG_S7(sp)
  ld s8, OFFSET_REG_S8(sp)
  ld s9, OFFSET_REG_S9(sp)
  ld s10, OFFSET_REG_S10(sp)
  ld s11, OFFSET_REG_S11(sp)
  ld t3, OFFSET_REG_T3(sp)
  ld t4, OFFSET_REG_T4(sp)
  ld t5, OFFSET_REG_T5(sp)
  ld t6, OFFSET_REG_T6(sp)

  ld t0, OFFSET_REG_SSTATUS(sp)
  csrw CSR_SSTATUS, t0
  ld t0, OFFSET_REG_SEPC(sp)
  csrw CSR_SEPC, t0
  ld t0, OFFSET_REG_STVAL(sp)
  csrw CSR_STVAL, t0
  ld t0, OFFSET_REG_SCAUSE(sp)
  csrw CSR_SCAUSE, t0
  ld t0, OFFSET_REG_SSCRATCH(sp)
  csrw CSR_SSCRATCH, t0

  addi sp, sp, (OFFSET_SIZE)
  sd sp, PCB_KERNEL_SP(tp)
.endm

/* 
 * trick: during an irq handling, current_running may be modified
 * but $tp will not be modified until ret_from_exception()
 */
ENTRY(enable_preempt)
  ld t0, PCB_PREEMPT_COUNT(tp)
  beq t0, zero, do_enable
  addi t0, t0, -1
  sd t0, PCB_PREEMPT_COUNT(tp)
  beq t0, zero, do_enable
  jr ra
do_enable:
  not t0, x0
  csrs CSR_SIE, t0
  jr ra
ENDPROC(enable_preempt)

ENTRY(disable_preempt)
  csrw CSR_SIE, zero  
  ld t0, PCB_PREEMPT_COUNT(tp)
  addi t0, t0, 1
  sd t0, PCB_PREEMPT_COUNT(tp)
  jr ra
ENDPROC(disable_preempt)

ENTRY(enable_interrupt)
  li t0, SR_SIE
  csrs CSR_SSTATUS, t0
  jr ra
ENDPROC(enable_interrupt)

ENTRY(disable_interrupt)
  li t0, SR_SIE
  csrc CSR_SSTATUS, t0
  jr ra
ENDPROC(disable_interrupt)

ENTRY(enable_sum)
  li t0, SR_SUM
  csrs CSR_SSTATUS, t0
  jr ra
ENDPROC(enable_sum)

ENTRY(disable_sum)
  li t0, SR_SUM
  csrc CSR_SSTATUS, t0
  jr ra
ENDPROC(disable_sum)

ENTRY(ret_from_exception)
  ld tp, current_cpu_running
  call unlock_kernel
  RESTORE_CONTEXT

  csrrw tp, CSR_SSCRATCH, tp
  bnez tp, to_user
to_kernel:
  csrrw tp, CSR_SSCRATCH, tp
  ld sp, PCB_KERNEL_SP(tp)
  j restore_sp_done
to_user:
  ld sp, PCB_USER_SP(tp)
restore_sp_done:
  sret
ENDPROC(ret_from_exception)

ENTRY(exception_handler_entry)
  /* use kernel stack to handle exception */
  csrrw tp, CSR_SSCRATCH, tp
  bnez tp, from_user

from_kernel:
  csrrw tp, CSR_SSCRATCH, tp
  j store_sp_done
from_user:
  sd sp, PCB_USER_SP(tp)
  ld sp, PCB_KERNEL_SP(tp)
store_sp_done:

  SAVE_CONTEXT
  /* 
   * Disable user-mode memory access as it should only be set in the actual user copy routines.
   * Disable the FPU to detect illegal usage of floating point in kernel space.
   */
  li t0, SR_SUM | SR_FS
  csrc sstatus, t0

  /* load the global pointer */
  .option push
  .option norelax
  la gp, __global_pointer$
  .option pop

  call lock_kernel
  /* 
   * load ret_from_exception into $ra
   * so that we can return to ret_from_exception
   * when interrupt_helper complete.
   */
  la ra, ret_from_exception
  
  /* call interrupt_helper and pass parameters for it */
  mv a0, sp
  csrr a1, CSR_STVAL
  csrr a2, CSR_SCAUSE
  j interrupt_helper
ENDPROC(exception_handler_entry)

ENTRY(clear_ipi)
  li t0, SIE_SSIE
  csrc CSR_SIP, t0
  jr ra
ENDPROC(clear_ipi)

content.text: I've completed the analysis. Here are my findings.

findings.title: Interrupt-mode do_net_recv copies the staged frames out *before* it actually waits
findings.detail:
In this kernel `scheduler()` does not switch stacks. `exception_handler_entry` sets `ra = ret_from_exception` and the real context switch happens in `ret_from_exception` (`ld tp, current_cpu_running` + `RESTORE_CONTEXT`, arch/riscv/kernel/entry.S:156-163). Therefore every line after a `scheduler()` call keeps executing immediately, in the same syscall invocation, on the still-current kernel stack — the task only stops running when the syscall path finally returns.

The rest of the codebase is built around that fact: `binsem_op()` (kernel/locking/binsem.c:38-45) has the *unlocker* fill in `binsem_id` for the heir instead of letting the woken task do it, and `do_waitpid()` rewinds `regs->sepc` by 4 so the `ecall` is re-executed after wakeup (kernel/sched/sched.c:416).

`do_net_recv()` ignores this. Lines 78-93 do `do_block(...); scheduler();` and then immediately run the copy-out loop and `return rx_tail;`. At that moment `XEmacPsRecvHandler()` has not run, `recv_stage`/`recv_stage_len` are still all zero, so the loop copies nothing, `*frLength[i]` is set to 0 and `handle_syscall` stores `rx_tail == 0` into the blocked task's saved `a0`. Later the RX interrupt fires, the handler fills `recv_stage` and unblocks the task — but the task resumes *after* the syscall and never re-reads the staging buffer.
findings.why_wrong: `test/recv.c` run with mode 1 (`recv <n> 1`) prints `sys_net_recv(...)` = 0 and dumps an empty `recv_buffer`; no received packet ever reaches user space in interrupt mode. The poll-mode path (lines 56-71) is unaffected because it copies before yielding.
findings.suggested_fix: Use the codebase's retry idiom: give `do_net_recv` the trailing `regs_context_t *regs` argument that `handle_syscall` already passes, and on the first call arm the transaction, `do_block`, rewind `regs->sepc -= 4` and `scheduler()`; on the retried call notice that the staging buffer is ready (e.g. a `recv_done` flag set by `XEmacPsRecvHandler`) and only then perform the copy-out and return the length. Alternatively point `_addr`/`_frLength` straight at the user buffer while the caller's `pgdir` is still installed — but that only works if the interrupt is guaranteed to be taken in the same address space, which it is not, so the retry approach is the safe one.

findings.title: P5 stores the pending-kill mark in pcb->status, where do_block()/do_unblock() erase it
findings.detail:
P5 marks a victim that is running on the other hart by writing `victim->status = TASK_KILLED` (line 367; the same marker is used by `do_exit()` at line 320) and `scheduler()` tears the task down only when it observes `prev->status == TASK_KILLED` (line 66).

P4 deliberately does *not* do this. It keeps the mark in a separate array and says so explicitly at Project4-Virtual_Memory_Management/kernel/sched/sched.c:47-54: "The mark lives outside the pcb because `status` is overwritten by every do_block()". P4 uses `pending_kill[NR_CPUS]` (P4 line 54, set at P4 line 452, consumed at P4 line 84).

In P5 the marker is lost by any of `do_block()` (line 597 sets `TASK_BLOCKED`), `do_unblock()` (line 605 sets `TASK_READY`) or `scheduler()` itself (line 83 sets `TASK_RUNNING`).
findings.why_wrong: Hart A runs `do_kill(pid)` for a task currently executing on hart B; it sets `TASK_KILLED` and returns 1 ("Task killed" is printed by the shell). Before its next timer tick the victim traps into the kernel and calls `sys_sleep` / `binsem_op(LOCK)` / `sys_waitpid`, all of which call `do_block()` and overwrite the status with `TASK_BLOCKED`. When that hart reaches `scheduler()`, `prev->status` is neither `TASK_RUNNING` nor `TASK_KILLED`, so the `dying` branch never fires: the address space is never freed, the pcb is never reclaimed, and the task is woken again later and keeps running even though `release_resources()` has already stripped it (see the separate finding on line 362).
findings.suggested_fix: Port P4's `static pcb_t * volatile pending_kill[NR_CPUS];` mechanism: in `do_kill()` set `pending_kill[victim->cpu_id] = victim` instead of touching `status`, and in `scheduler()` test `if (pending_kill[cpu_id] == prev) { pending_kill[cpu_id] = NULL; dying = prev; }` before the `TASK_RUNNING` re-queue test (P4 sched.c:83-93).

findings.title: do_kill() runs release_resources() on a victim that is still executing on the other hart
findings.detail:
P5's `do_kill()` calls `release_resources(victim)` unconditionally at line 362, before it even checks whether the victim is still running (line 364). P4 does the opposite: `release_resources()` is only reached from `destroy_task()` (P4 sched.c:359-361), which the *owning* hart calls out of `scheduler()` once `satp` no longer points at the victim. P4 documents the reason at sched.c:449-451: "It is running on the other hart ... and it may still be inside a critical section, so nothing may be taken away yet."

`release_resources()` -> `release_binsem()` (line 260-274) walks `task->binsem_id[]`, does `node->sem++` for each and hands the lock to the next waiter via `do_unblock()`.
findings.why_wrong: Kill a task that holds a binary semaphore while it is running on the other hart. `release_binsem()` immediately grants that semaphore to another waiter, but the victim keeps executing (and, per the TASK_KILLED finding, may never be destroyed at all) inside what it believes is still its critical section — two tasks now hold the same mutex. When the victim eventually reaches `binsem_op(BINSEM_OP_UNLOCK)` it does `node->sem++` a second time (sem goes to 2, mutual exclusion permanently broken) and `current_running[cpu_id]->binsem_num--` on an already-zero counter, leaving `binsem_num == -1`, which makes the next `binsem_op(LOCK)` write `binsem_id[-1]` — an out-of-bounds store into the pcb.
findings.suggested_fix: Move the `release_resources(victim)` call out of `do_kill()` and into the teardown path that runs on the victim's own hart, exactly as P4 does: keep it as the first statement of a `destroy_task()`-style helper that is invoked from `scheduler()` (for the running case) and directly from `do_kill()` (for the ready/blocked case).

findings.title: P5 dropped abandon_binsem_wait(): killing a task queued on a binsem permanently unbalances sem
findings.detail:
P4 has a helper `abandon_binsem_wait()` (Project4-Virtual_Memory_Management/kernel/sched/sched.c:317-336) that scans every `binsem_nodes[i].block_queue` for the dying task, removes it and does `node->sem++`, and calls it from `release_resources()` (P4 line 343). P5's `release_resources()` (lines 278-288) only calls `release_binsem()`; the helper is gone entirely.

`binsem_op(BINSEM_OP_LOCK)` decrements `node->sem` *before* blocking (kernel/locking/binsem.c:36-40), so a task sitting on `block_queue` owns one unit of that negative count. P5's `reclaim_pcb()` (line 297) does `list_del(&task->list)`, which silently pulls the victim off the binsem queue without giving the count back.
findings.why_wrong: Task B blocks on binsem k (`sem` goes from 0 to -1, B is on `block_queue`). Task B is killed: `reclaim_pcb()` removes B from the queue, `sem` stays -1 and the queue is now empty. Holder A then calls `binsem_op(k, UNLOCK)`: `sem++` makes it 0, the test `if (node->sem <= 0)` is true, and binsem.c:51-55 does `list_entry(node->block_queue.next, pcb_t, list)` on the *list head itself*, producing a bogus `pcb_t*` pointing into `binsem_nodes[]`. It then writes `unblocked_pcb->binsem_id[...]` through that pointer and `do_unblock()`s the fake node onto `ready_queue`, which the scheduler will later dispatch. Kernel memory corruption / crash.
findings.suggested_fix: Copy P4's `abandon_binsem_wait()` verbatim into P5's sched.c and call it from `release_resources()` right after `release_binsem(task)`.

findings.title: write_to_sd() only flushes the local TLB; P4 does a remote shootdown
findings.detail:
P4's `write_to_sd()` ends with `flush_tlb_all()` (Project4-Virtual_Memory_Management/kernel/mm/mm.c:147), which is `local_flush_tlb_all() + sbi_remote_sfence_vma(NULL, 0, -1)`. P5 replaced every `flush_tlb_all()` with `local_flush_tlb_all()` (mm.c:161, 269, 346, 373, 400) because P5's arch/riscv/include/pgtable.h no longer defines the `flush_tlb_all()` wrapper — but `sbi_remote_sfence_vma()` is still available (arch/riscv/include/sbi.h:104).

The other four sites are benign (they touch only the current process's mappings, and `set_satp()` issues an `sfence.vma` on every context switch). `write_to_sd()` is different: `selete_page()` picks a victim frame belonging to *any* process, including one that is currently running in user mode on the other hart.
findings.why_wrong: Hart 0 is in the kernel (holding `kernel_lock`) and needs a frame; `alloc_user_page()` -> `selete_page()` -> `write_to_sd()` picks a frame owned by process B, which is running in user mode on hart 1. The PTE loses `_PAGE_PRESENT` and `free_user_page()` puts the frame back in the pool, but only hart 0's TLB is invalidated. Hart 1 keeps using its cached translation and reads/writes a frame that has already been handed to (and `memset` to zero by) another process — silent cross-process corruption and data leakage.
findings.suggested_fix: Replace the `local_flush_tlb_all()` at mm.c:161 with a remote shootdown: `local_flush_tlb_all(); sbi_remote_sfence_vma(NULL, 0, -1);` (or re-add the `flush_tlb_all()` inline to P5's pgtable.h and use it there).

findings.title: P5 dropped the pending_reap deferral: the kernel stack is published for reuse while it is still in use
findings.detail:
P4 keeps a `pending_reap[NR_CPUS]` array (Project4-Virtual_Memory_Management/kernel/sched/sched.c:56-62, 78-81, 373-379) so that an `AUTO_CLEANUP_ON_EXIT` task is only handed to core 0's reaper one full scheduling round after it stopped running. The comment explains why: "which frees its kernel stack -- the very stack the dying task is still standing on while it unwinds out of the kernel".

P5's `reclaim_pcb()` publishes it immediately: `list_add_tail(&task->list, &kernel_pcb[0].wait_list)` (line 304), reached from `scheduler()` at line 101.
findings.why_wrong: `scheduler()` runs on the dying task's kernel stack and returns onto it (do_exit's epilogue, handle_syscall's epilogue, `unlock_kernel`, and the first instructions of `ret_from_exception` all execute with `sp` inside that page). Core 0's idle loop (init/main.c:243-250) runs *without* `kernel_lock`, so as soon as hart 1 appends the pcb, core 0 can call `free_user_page(kva2pa(clean_pcb->kernel_stack_base - PAGE_SIZE))`. The next `alloc_user_page()` hands that frame out and `memset`s it to zero (mm.c:73) while hart 1 is still unwinding on it — the saved `ra`/`s0` on that stack are zeroed and hart 1 jumps to 0.
findings.suggested_fix: Port P4's `pending_reap[NR_CPUS]`: in `reclaim_pcb()` store the task in `pending_reap[cpu_id]` instead of appending it, and at the top of `scheduler()` move `pending_reap[cpu_id]` onto `kernel_pcb[0].wait_list` (P4 sched.c:77-81).

findings.title: do_kill()/do_waitpid() can match an unused pcb slot because the pid < 0 guard is missing
findings.detail:
P4 funnels both lookups through `find_pcb()` (Project4-Virtual_Memory_Management/kernel/sched/sched.c:409-422), whose first statement is `if (pid < 0) return NULL; /* -1 is the free-slot marker, never a real process */`. P5 kept the raw open-coded loops in `do_kill()` (lines 342-348) and `do_waitpid()` (lines 391-397) with no such guard.

Unused pcb slots are marked by `pcb[i].pid = -1` (init/main.c:104) and everything else in them is BSS zero: `status == TASK_BLOCKED` (enum value 0), `mode == ENTER_ZOMBIE_ON_EXIT` (0), and `wait_list == {NULL, NULL}` — never passed through `init_list_head()`.
findings.why_wrong: `sys_kill(-1)` (reachable from the shell: `atoi()` in tiny_libc/string.c:80 has no sign handling, so e.g. `kill /` yields exactly -1) selects the first pristine slot. Its status is 0 == TASK_BLOCKED, so none of the early-out tests fire, and `release_resources()` runs: `list_empty(&task->wait_list)` compares `NULL == &wait_list` and returns false, so `do_unblock(task->wait_list.next)` is called with NULL and `list_del(NULL)` dereferences `entry->prev` at address 0. The resulting kernel-mode load fault re-enters `exception_handler_entry`, which calls `lock_kernel()` on the already-held big kernel lock — self-deadlock, machine hangs. `do_waitpid(-1)` on an already-reaped slot double-frees the kernel stack via `free_user_page(kva2pa(child->kernel_stack_base - PAGE_SIZE))` at line 407.
findings.suggested_fix: Add P4's `find_pcb()` helper (with the `pid < 0` early return) and use it in both `do_kill()` and `do_waitpid()` instead of the inline loops.

findings.title: init_user_stack() has no page budget, so long argv can scribble past the single mapped stack page
findings.detail:
Only one page of user stack is mapped when the process is created (`alloc_page_helper(top_va - PAGE_SIZE, ...)`, line 138) and everything is written through `STACK_KVA(va) = top_kva - (top_va - va)`, i.e. through the kernel direct map of that one frame. P5 walks the strings with no size accounting at all (lines 154-169).

P4 added an explicit clamp for exactly this (Project4-Virtual_Memory_Management/kernel/sched/sched.c:171-184): it measures the strings first and drops arguments from the tail while `need + sizeof(uintptr_t) * (argc + 2) > PAGE_SIZE - 64`.
findings.why_wrong: If the strings plus the `argc + 1` pointer array exceed ~4 KiB, `sp` drops below `top_va - PAGE_SIZE` and `STACK_KVA(sp)` walks below `top_kva - PAGE_SIZE`, i.e. into the *previous physical frame* in the kernel direct map — which belongs to an unrelated process (or is a page table / kernel stack). The `memcpy` at line 158 and the `slot[]` stores at lines 165-169 corrupt it silently, and the new process's `sp` points at an unmapped user address. The bundled shell caps this (`MAX_ARGC 10` x 100 chars, test/test_shell.c:38,120) so it is not reachable from `test_shell`, but any user program calling `sys_exec` with longer arguments hits it.
findings.suggested_fix: Port P4's budget loop verbatim into P5's `init_user_stack()`.

findings.title: do_exec() passes the unclamped argc to init_pcb_stack() while init_user_stack() clamps its own copy
findings.detail: P5 clamps `argc` locally inside `init_user_stack()` (lines 147-152, by value), but `do_exec()` then passes the *original*, unclamped `argc` to `init_pcb_stack()` at line 249, which loads it into `a0`. P4 moved the clamp up into `do_exec()` before either call (Project4-Virtual_Memory_Management/kernel/sched/sched.c:231-238) and additionally has `init_user_stack()` write the effective count back through `int *argc_io`, with the comment "clamp once, so that the array built on the user stack and the `argc` handed to main() can never disagree".
findings.why_wrong: `sys_exec(name, argc, argv, mode)` with `argc > MAX_EXEC_ARGC` (16) builds a 17-entry NULL-terminated array on the user stack but starts the process with `a0 = argc`, so `main()` reads `argv[16..argc-1]` past the NULL terminator — garbage pointers that the callee will dereference. Likewise `sys_exec(name, 3, NULL, mode)` builds an argv of just `{NULL}` but still hands `a0 = 3` to `main()`.
findings.suggested_fix: Hoist the `argc < 0 || argv == NULL` and `argc > MAX_EXEC_ARGC` clamps out of `init_user_stack()` into `do_exec()` before `init_user_stack()`/`init_pcb_stack()` are called (or change `init_user_stack()` to take `int *argc_io` as P4 does).
